question: Your extraction system processes vendor invoices and adds anomaly flags in three categories for the accounts payable team: duplicate line items, missing tax IDs, and unusual payment terms. An audit shows that most unusual-payment-terms flags are false positives, while the other two categories are almost always accurate. The accounts payable team now dismisses all flags without reading them, including correct duplicate-line-item flags. What should you do first to restore the team's trust in the flags?

options.text: Turn off all three anomaly categories until the prompts for every category have been rewritten and tested against a new set of invoices.
options.reason: The guide targets only the high false-positive categories for temporary disabling; turning off the two accurate categories removes reliable flags without need.

options.text: Disable the unusual-payment-terms category temporarily and keep the other two categories active while you rewrite its prompt with explicit criteria for which terms to flag.
options.reason: The guide recommends temporarily disabling high false-positive categories to restore trust while improving the prompts for those categories, and keeping the accurate categories in use.

options.text: Add an instruction to the prompt for all three categories that tells Claude to be conservative and report only anomalies it is highly confident about.
options.reason: The guide states that general instructions like 'be conservative' or 'only report high-confidence findings' fail to improve precision compared to specific categorical criteria.

options.text: Keep all three categories active and tell the accounts payable team that unusual-payment-terms flags are less reliable than the other flags.
options.reason: The guide states that a high false-positive category undermines confidence in the accurate categories, so keeping it active continues to erode trust instead of restoring it.
